biur-halacha/1:ב: And likewise if it touched etc. — at first glance this has no explanation, namely this; and I found in Mateh Yehudah who forced an explanation and wrote that one can say: since in other prohibitions in Yoreh De'ah siman 105 only touching of roasting is mentioned — the way they roasted with its fat or a piece that was roasted with the forbidden substance — and heat of its surface is not mentioned there, therefore he wrote "and likewise if chametz bread touched" etc., meaning: in the first clause, heat of its roasting, and in the second clause heat of its surface — in both only the place of contact is forbidden. And know that heat of its roasting here means there is only touching alone; but that which is below siman 467 subsection 15, that there are those who forbid the entire thing, deals with roasting by a spit, for when one turns the spit the taste spreads through the entire thing, as explained there — end of his words. And in my humble opinion it appears it should read "and therefore."
biur-halacha/1:ג: And there is no permeating substance etc. alone — see Magen Avraham in subsection 2 at its end, who wrote that the law of its surface is like roasting; nevertheless it appears to me one should rule here as Rama wrote in salting in siman 467 seif 14, that in any case roasting is not better than salting; and see in Peri Megadim who wrote that although the Rav was silent here on what the Mechaber wrote "there is no permeating substance, only the place of contact is forbidden," I do not agree except he relied on 467 seif 14 regarding salting, that they forbid that entire piece b'eyna in sixty, and on Pesach in any amount; and in truth such is Bach's view there in siman 461. In practice one should look, for Peri Chadash below in siman 461 and Gra in this siman and Maamar Mordechai in siman 461 — all their view is to be lenient like Shulchan Aruch's ruling; and therefore their reason is specifically in salting, where the forbidden substance is found on the meat, where sometimes it is fatty [and also because we do not know at which place the contact was, therefore they are stringent on that piece]; not so in our matter with two loaves where fattiness does not apply at all — one need not be stringent. However Eshel Avraham's view is like Bach, and I found several other Acharonim who copied Bach's words; and all this is only because of the stringency of chametz — people are accustomed to be stringent; and it appears that in a place of loss one may rely to be lenient in this. Afterwards I found in Yoreh De'ah siman 105 in Peri Megadim in Sha'ar HaTevunah section 38 who also sides to be lenient in a place of loss regarding a weak forbidden substance that has no fattiness at all.
biur-halacha/1:ד: And there are those who are stringent etc. — Mateh Yehudah wrote: it appears one should be stringent only in something uncommon, for example if chametz bread was baked on Pesach with fatty meat — in this one should be stringent, because although it is not a common thing in any amount, nevertheless there is a concern; but in something common, such as wheat found in one of the dishes in an oven, there is no reason to be stringent even in a completely sealed oven where reicha applies, for this is less than two rabbinic any-amounts that the Acharonim spoke of — for even from actual fatty meat it is not [according to what we hold fully absorbed] except any amount, and this smell coming from the wheat, even if its entire body became mixed, is only any amount and through smell; and according to Yerushalmi and Ramban to Levi, in truth even any amount is not certain in such a case — it is not worth relying on the question to permit, especially in a place preventing Yom Tov joy; and there is no proof from Tosafot who are stringent even regarding wheat, for they rule like Rav that reicha is a matter; etc. — see there where he elaborated and concludes thus for practical law.
biur-halacha/1:ה: Where reicha applies — see Mishna Berurah in what he wrote "but in a thing where the name reicha does not apply" etc.; and regarding cooking see Magen Avraham who concludes that what the Rav was stringent about in Yoreh De'ah siman 108 seif 2 in the gloss regarding when the oven was completely sealed, even in cooking [unless in great loss], deals specifically with hot foods insulated for Shabbat, for since they remain a long time inside the oven and the oven is sealed on every side, their smell is strong and its law is like roasting; but in ordinary cooking, even if they remain an hour or two, one need not be stringent. And regarding Pesach see what is written in Mishna Berurah.
biur-halacha/2:א: Chametz that became mixed etc. like other prohibitions — from the Mechaber's stam wording it is implied that even in its own kind its law is so, that sixty suffices and it is not called chametz — a thing that has a permitted form because next year it returns and becomes forbidden, according to the first view brought in Yoreh De'ah siman 102 in the gloss — see there; and so ruled Taz and in Sefer Api Ravrevi; and not like Shach there subsection 13 who wrote the Mechaber refers only to not in its own kind [Rabbi Akiva Eiger], and so stam Levush here and Magen Avraham subsection 40, and so Gra in Yoreh De'ah there — the Mechaber is stam here like the first view there that chametz is not called a davar sheyesh lo matirin.
biur-halacha/2:ג: Also permitted. Shibolei Leket wrote: leaven or chametz that fell into a pot or was cooked with roasted meat — it gives taste for detriment and is permitted, end of his words. Behold Shibolei Leket abbreviated the language and there is room to err; therefore I will copy his wording: in sign 217, leaven or chametz that fell into a pot or was cooked with roasted meat — we know in it that it gives taste for detriment in that food and is permitted, even though that food has chametz taste, for chametz b'eyna is fit for its purpose and is not spoiled, for it is visible for its matter that it is forbidden, etc., since its taste is spoiled and spoils in this food it is permitted — end of his words. And it is implied from his language that he was precise to write cooked with roasted meat, but with cooked meat it is not for detriment [and not like Magen Avraham implies that he does not distinguish in this]; and even if it fell into a dish, not in every dough that fell into a dish do we say it is for detriment, but in something very sour that is not customary to put in a dish — in this we say it is presumably spoiled [and with this the difficulty of Beit HaTovim from Yoreh De'ah siman 323 is resolved, where it says if dough of challah fell into a dish it forbids]. And see Chok Yaakov who challenged Magen Avraham, and Rabbi Akiva Eiger resolved it that presumably here too it is for detriment; and according to what we explained, Shibolei Leket's intent is not in every chametz, but in that which is very sour. And perhaps he too agrees in this for practical law. And regarding grain kernels found in a well of water on Pesach whether this is called taste for detriment, see Magen Avraham and Rabbi Akiva Eiger and Peri Megadim, and it will be explained below in siman 467 seif 13. And regarding dough of chametz that fell into a well see below siman 467 seif 12 in Mishna Berurah s.v. ein.
biur-halacha/4:ג: Wet — see in Chemed Moshe who proved that what Rama wrote wet in wet is not precise that both were wet, but if only the chametz was wet, even if the permitted substance is dry, it also does not revive — see there.
biur-halacha/5:ה: Forbidden by law if they were not careful etc. and that they did not melt etc. — see Magen Avraham subsection 21 who explains Rama's words that it is not permitted by law unless they were careful in both matters; and explanation is needed, for in cheeses he was not concerned b'dieved about chametz crumbs, only to be stringent l'chatchila; and I saw in Mateh Yehudah who elaborated on this, and his view is that Rama's main point that it is forbidden by law is only because of concern for discharge from chametz vessels, and he forced Rama's language greatly — see there; and in my humble opinion Rama was stringent only regarding fat, b'dieved because of chametz crumbs, similar to what Chok Yaakov wrote in subsection 30 in the name of Mahari"t that it is customary to gather etc. — see there; and therefore crumbs of chametz are found in it; but in other things Rama truly mentioned only concern for chametz vessels, and so is proven in Darkei Moshe that preserves are permitted if made in the designated vessel, and he wrote explicitly that because of chametz crumbs we are not concerned; and so Acharonim copied stam; and also from Magen Avraham in subsection 26 it is implied only in fat we are concerned for crumbs even b'dieved, not in cooked wine and the like — see there; however from Chok Yaakov in subsection 33 it is implied he does not distinguish in this; and see in Shulchan Aruch of Gra section 47, and this requires study.
biur-halacha/5:ו: And likewise anything etc. — know that there are Poskim who hold specifically regarding fat, that the pan in which they melt it is customarily used constantly, and likewise similar cases regarding pots used frequently — presumably they are ben yomo until you know they are not ben yomo; but in other vessels we say presumably they are not ben yomo [and this is Mahari"t's view, agreed by Kenesset HaGedolah and Peri Chadash]; nevertheless from Shulchan Aruch and Acharonim it is implied that because of chametz stringency we are stringent in every case. And regarding mixtures, Magen Avraham's view in subsection 26 is to be lenient in wine and vinegar except fat because crumbs do not usually mix into them, even if they became mixed in less than sixty; and Chok Yaakov's view in subsection 32 implies in all things one is not lenient except in great loss; and it appears one may rely on Magen Avraham's view since Mahari"t and his supporters are lenient in stam vessels even without mixtures; and likewise in fat one may rely on Chok Yaakov to be lenient in great loss, for several Acharonim copied his words for halachah [Gra and Magen Alef and Makor Chayim]; and also implied in Gra's explanation there that the essential law is stringency — see there.
biur-halacha/5:ז: That they cook in chametz vessels etc. — see in Beit Meir who elaborated and wrote that he means at least it is known that it was cooked, even if there is doubt whether it was a chametz vessel — we presume all vessels stam are chametz vessels if it is not known they have designated vessels; but if there is doubt whether it was cooked at all, such as the herb called tea — what prohibition concern is there; and I heard people say the reason is perhaps it is counterfeit, what was already determined boiled and dried; but in this both reasons of Rabbenu Tam (brought in Beit Yosef) apply — from where do we presume prohibition, and also we taste it all year etc.; and in this there is no concern the counterfeit was made on Pesach and there is any amount in it, for it comes from a distant land; and why not say everything separated from the majority is separated — see there where he elaborated and concludes in my humble opinion it is only like things permitted and others practiced prohibition by mistake.
biur-halacha/5:ט: He must destroy it — and regarding wine whether it is permitted to drink it, at first glance the matter is simple that before two months when it already dried and does not give taste in wine, one pours the wine from the barrel and it is permitted to drink, and all the more to retain; and if within two months when it gives taste in wine that Rama forbade drinking — regarding retaining it depends on the two resolutions in Magen Avraham subsection 30: according to the first resolution it is forbidden, according to the second permitted; and it appears the second resolution is primary.
biur-halacha/7:_: Unripe grapes crushed before Pesach — from this wording it is implied that during Pesach one may not be lenient; and the reason is because of what Semak concluded at the end of his words "and even if it discharges" etc. [as brought by Taz]; therefore according to this it is permitted only before Pesach, and Rama decided for practical law like the first part of his words that it does not discharge when cold, and therefore even during Pesach it is permitted [Mordechai]; however it is difficult, for Rama should have written "and some say" or "it appears to me," not stam; and Mateh Yehudah already challenged this and it remains in difficulty; and in my humble opinion if we hold for practical law like Eshel Avraham and Netziv that before Pesach it is permitted when crushed even if the mortar was not clean — it is simple the Mechaber deals when the vessel was not clean, and therefore they permit only before Pesach; and Rama's language fits very well for one who examines and understands.
biur-halacha/8:א: If it is not ben yomo etc. — see Mishna Berurah that if it is ben yomo it is forbidden, and so in Tur; and see Rabbi Akiva Eiger and other Acharonim who noted that through pickling it is never ben yomo, for the absorption of the forbidden substance or chametz is completed before the absorption of the pickled item placed afterward; and so Magen Avraham above in seif 5 wrote there that it cannot be conceived to forbid through pickling except when it was b'eyna — at the moment they removed the chametz at that moment they placed the pickled item, and this is forced, for then Tur and Mechaber should have explained and not been stam; and Chok Yaakov wrote that in our matter it is forbidden because of absorption, since there is some sharpness; and this too is forced, for Tur wrote stam that with water their sharpness is nullified; nevertheless for practical law it appears to be stringent, for Beit HaLevi in siman 69 and Peri Chadash resolved Taz's and Shach's difficulty that a vessel standing with gravy never loses its taste forever, only when empty it loses taste; and according to them Shulchan Aruch's words come for practical law according to their plain meaning; and so in Sefer Maamar Mordechai; and even though several Acharonim copied Taz's and Shach's words for halachah, nevertheless it does not appear to be lenient l'chatchila, especially here where Chok Yaakov also wrote for prohibition and Makor Chayim copied; however in time of pressure it appears one may rely to be lenient also in this, for otherwise Chok Yaakov's view above in sign 19 is not to forbid through pickling except in a vessel used frequently for chametz, when one must estimate against the whole; if not, we say there are sixty against its discharge — see there.
biur-halacha/11:_: Whether chametz etc. — see Mishna Berurah where I wrote: if it became mixed in less than sixty etc. — according to his view, through chametz mixtures of a kezayit, so it is in the beginning of siman 442 in Magen Avraham — see there: if there is not sixty against a kezayit, according to all one does not transgress bal yera'eh; and so Gra brought in this siman; and I did not copy what Magen Avraham brought in the name of Bach, that if it became mixed in less than sixty, even if there was not a kezayit, one does not transgress bal yera'eh, nevertheless for eating it is forbidden after Pesach because chametz taste in pieces is forbidden without redemption, because Beit Meir questioned this since one did not transgress bal yera'eh on this mixture, why should it not be permitted in eating (and taste of chametz in pieces does not apply after Pesach); and so implied in Gra's explanation in subsection 39 that the Mechaber who requires sixty deals when there is at least a kezayit; and in subsection 41 it is implied that regarding mixtures on which one did not transgress bal yera'eh, it is permitted in eating and benefit, even without redemption — and this is even without redemption that the Mechaber does not deal with this; however Makor Chayim's view here is like Magen Avraham, that even less than a kezayit is forbidden without redemption, and his reason is because many Poskim hold one transgresses bal yera'eh also on less than a kezayit; and perhaps Gra also holds one transgresses bal yera'eh even on less than a kezayit, but this is specifically when it is b'eyna and not through mixtures — and this requires study for practical law.
